description: The six hazard classes Groundwork's detector is trained on. This file is the single source of truth: the database enum, the rulebook triggers, and the training data.yaml all have to agree with it, and a test fails if they drift.

classes.name: dead_vegetation
classes.label: Dead vegetation
classes.definition: Standing or fallen plant material that is visibly dead or fully cured: brown/grey shrubs with no green growth, dried annual grass, dead branches still attached to a living plant, accumulated leaf litter on the ground.
include: A shrub that is brown throughout with no living foliage
Cured annual grass, straw-coloured, in a mowed or unmowed area
Dead branches within an otherwise living shrub or tree
Leaf and needle litter accumulated on the ground within 30 feet of a structure
exclude: A deciduous plant that is merely dormant and has visible live buds or twig flexibility
Bare soil or gravel with no plant material
Cut and bagged green waste awaiting collection
Brown mulch, which is combustible_mulch_z0 when in the first five feet
classes.source: PRC 4291(a)(1); CSFS Home Ignition Zone guide
classes.notes: The commonest failure is confusing cured grass with bare dry soil. If individual stems are visible, it is vegetation.

classes.name: veg_touching_structure
classes.label: Vegetation touching the structure
classes.definition: Living or dead vegetation in physical contact with an exterior wall, eave, window, door frame, or roof edge.
include: A shrub whose foliage presses against siding
A vine growing on or up a wall
Tree foliage resting on an eave or gutter
A hedge planted flush to the wall with no visible gap
exclude: A plant near the wall with visible daylight between it and the siding — that is a Zone 0 setback question, not contact
Vegetation touching a detached fence rather than the house
Potted plants on a patio not against the wall
classes.source: IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home; draft Zone 0
classes.notes: Contact is the whole criterion. When contact is ambiguous from the angle, do not label it — a false positive here reads as an accusation.

classes.name: overhanging_limbs
classes.label: Overhanging limbs
classes.definition: Tree limbs extending over a roof surface, chimney, or stovepipe outlet.
include: A branch whose vertical projection falls on the roof plane
Limbs above or adjacent to a chimney outlet
Branches over a deck roof or porch cover attached to the house
exclude: Trees beside a structure whose limbs stop short of the roofline
Limbs over a detached shed or over the street
Limbs over a driveway or lawn with no structure beneath
classes.notes: Judge from the projection, not apparent overlap: a telephoto angle makes a distant tree look like it sits on the roof.

classes.name: combustible_mulch_z0
classes.label: Combustible mulch in the first five feet
classes.definition: Bark, wood chip, or other combustible ground cover within roughly five feet of an exterior wall.
include: Shredded bark or wood chips in a planting bed against the house
Rubber mulch abutting the foundation
Straw or pine-needle ground cover in the same band
exclude: Gravel, decomposed granite, stone, or bare soil
Bark mulch clearly beyond the first five feet
Loose leaf litter, which is dead_vegetation
classes.notes: The five-foot band is judged relative to visible reference objects — a standard door is about 3 feet wide, a typical siding course 6-8 inches. Label only when the band is confidently in frame.

classes.name: attached_wood_fence
classes.label: Combustible fence attached to the house
classes.definition: A wooden fence, gate, trellis, or lattice that physically meets an exterior wall.
include: A wood fence terminating at the siding
A wooden gate hinged to the structure
Lattice or trellis fixed to the wall and continuous with a fence
exclude: A wooden fence that stops short of the house, or meets a metal post first
Metal, vinyl, or masonry fencing regardless of where it attaches
Freestanding lattice screens not continuous with a fence
classes.notes: The junction must be visible in the frame. A fence running out of shot toward the house is not a label.

classes.name: combustibles_under_deck
classes.label: Combustible material under a deck
classes.definition: Stored or accumulated combustible material in the space beneath a deck, porch, or raised floor.
include: Firewood, lumber, or cardboard stored under a deck
Outdoor furniture or plastic bins stowed underneath
Deep leaf litter accumulated in the under-deck space
exclude: An enclosed, skirted under-deck space with nothing visible inside
Material beside a deck rather than beneath it
Ground-level patios with no space underneath
classes.source: CSFS Home Ignition Zone guide; IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home
classes.notes: Requires seeing into the space. A dark under-deck area where nothing is discernible is not labelled — absence of evidence is not evidence of clearance.
